title: How Our Bodies Grow and Change
strapline: Baby photos next to today's faces — the astonishing news that you used to be that small.
intent: Children develop awareness of how people grow and change across a lifetime.
Comparing then and now builds a first, concrete sense of time passing.
Children take visible pride in what they can do now that they could not do as a baby.
Talking about families invites difference in naturally and respectfully.
Children build the vocabulary of age and sequence — baby, child, grown-up, older.
implementation: Share baby photos — staff photos work well, and children's own only where families have agreed.
Always offer an alternative for any child whose family cannot or would rather not send a photo.
Compare then and now: what could this baby do, what can you do now?
Model respectful discussion and steer firmly away from comments about size or looks.
Introduce and use the vocabulary: baby, toddler, child, grown-up, older, younger.
Celebrate growing independence — dressing, pouring, writing a name.
Extend to families: babies, big brothers, parents, grandparents all grow and change.
key_questions: What could you do when you were a baby? What can you do now?
Who is the youngest person in your family? Who is the oldest?
What do you think you will be able to do when you are five?
How have you changed since you started nursery?
What is something you learned to do all by yourself?

impact.text: Children remember and compare past and present — "when I was a baby...".
Children talk about their own family and notice that other families are different.
Children show visible pride in effort and in what they can now do.
Children recount events from their own life in rough sequence.
Children take up and use vocabulary of age and time.
Children manage their own body and belongings more independently.

enhancements: A height chart on the wall measured at the start and end of the year.
A "when I was a baby / now I can" book each child makes and illustrates.
A family visit from someone with a real baby, if a family is willing.
A timeline of a life laid out as pictures for children to order.
A comparison with the plant and egg activities — everything living grows and changes.
A handprint or footprint comparison with the Autumn 1 handprint display.

playing_exploring: Children pore over photographs and make their own discoveries in them.
Guessing who is who in the baby photos is an irresistible open puzzle.
active_learning: Children stay with a conversation about themselves and their family.
Pride in new skills motivates them to try the next thing.
creating_thinking: Children order events and people in time and reason about sequence.
They connect their own growing to plants and animals growing.
